title: Carciofi alla Giudia
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Whole artichokes deep-fried twice, first to cook through and then again to crisp, opening up into a golden flower with leaves that shatter like crisps — a jewel of Rome's historic Jewish quarter.
longDesc: This centuries-old technique from Rome's Jewish community involves flattening the artichoke like a flower and frying it twice at different temperatures, the second, hotter fry being what gives the outer leaves their distinctive shattering crispness while the heart stays tender.
ingredients: 8 young, tender artichokes with long stems
Vegetable oil, for frying (enough to submerge the artichokes)
steps: Trim the tough outer leaves of each artichoke, peel the stem, and trim the top.
Place the trimmed artichokes in a bowl of water with lemon juice to prevent browning.
Using your hands, gently open and flatten each artichoke by pressing down and spreading the leaves outward like a flower.
Heat vegetable oil to 150°C (300°F) and fry the artichokes, stem-up, for about 10 minutes until tender when pierced.
Remove and let drain and rest briefly.
Fry the artichokes again briefly, about 2–3 minutes, until the outer leaves turn deeply golden and crisp — you can gently dunk them in the hot oil to help the leaves open further.
Drain, season generously with salt, and serve immediately while hot and crisp.
chefTips: Young, tender artichokes work best — older ones tend to have tougher, more fibrous centers.
The double-fry technique, at two distinct temperatures, is essential to achieving both a tender heart and shatteringly crisp outer leaves.
Serve immediately after the second fry, as the crispness fades relatively quickly.
commonMistakes: Using overly mature artichokes, which have tough, inedible chokes that are difficult to work around.
Skipping the double-fry technique, resulting in artichokes that are either undercooked inside or not properly crisp outside.
Letting the artichokes sit too long before the second fry, allowing them to cool and become less receptive to crisping.
servedWith: As part of a Roman antipasto spread
storage: Best eaten immediately; these do not hold or reheat well.
reheating: Not recommended; best enjoyed fresh and hot.
healthBenefits: Artichokes are a good source of fiber and antioxidants.
culturalNote: Carciofi alla giudia is a treasured specialty of Rome's ancient Jewish community, one of the oldest in Europe, and remains a beloved feature of the city's historic Ghetto district.
